Indefinite article (a / an).label: Sound, not spelling
Indefinite article (a / an).text: Teach 'a' before a consonant sound, 'an' before a vowel sound. Anchor it to pronunciation, not the letter.

Indefinite article (a / an).label: First mention
Indefinite article (a / an).text: Use 'a/an' to introduce something new and singular. Drill with classroom objects: 'It's a pen. It's an eraser.'

Indefinite article (a / an).label: Production
Indefinite article (a / an).text: Learners describe a bag's contents one item at a time, choosing a or an aloud.

Definite article (the).label: Shared knowledge
Definite article (the).text: Use 'the' when both speakers know which one. Contrast first vs second mention: 'I saw a dog. The dog was big.'

Definite article (the).label: One of a kind
Definite article (the).text: Introduce 'the' with unique things (the sun, the moon) and with superlatives later. Keep it concrete.

Definite article (the).label: Production
Definite article (the).text: Picture description: learners point and re-mention objects, switching from a/an to the.

Regular plurals (-s / -es).label: Three spoken endings
Regular plurals (-s / -es).text: Teach the three sounds of plural -s: /s/ (cats), /z/ (dogs), /iz/ (boxes). Listening discrimination drill.

Regular plurals (-s / -es).label: Spelling rules
Regular plurals (-s / -es).text: Add -es after s, x, z, ch, sh; change -y to -ies after a consonant (baby → babies). Sorting activity.

Regular plurals (-s / -es).label: Production
Regular plurals (-s / -es).text: Count and name multiple classroom objects, pronouncing the correct ending.

Irregular plurals (man/men, child/childr.label: Memorise as pairs
Irregular plurals (man/men, child/childr.text: Present the frequent irregulars as fixed pairs: man/men, woman/women, child/children, foot/feet, tooth/teeth, person/people.

Irregular plurals (man/men, child/childr.label: No -s trap
Irregular plurals (man/men, child/childr.text: Show that these take no plural -s. Drill with images and numbers: 'two feet', 'three children'.

Irregular plurals (man/men, child/childr.label: Production
Irregular plurals (man/men, child/childr.text: Describe a family photo using people, children, men, women.

Uncountable nouns (information, water).label: No a/an, no plural
Uncountable nouns (information, water).text: Introduce common uncountables (water, bread, money, information, advice, music). They take no a/an and no -s.

Uncountable nouns (information, water).label: Counting them
Uncountable nouns (information, water).text: Show measure phrases: a glass of water, a piece of advice, a slice of bread. Matching activity.

Uncountable nouns (information, water).label: Production
Uncountable nouns (information, water).text: Order food/drink using 'some + uncountable' and measure phrases.

The verb 'be' (am / is / are).label: Full paradigm first
The verb 'be' (am / is / are).text: Drill I am, you/we/they are, he/she/it is, plus contractions (I'm, he's). The pivot verb to automate.

The verb 'be' (am / is / are).label: Negatives & questions
The verb 'be' (am / is / are).text: Show inversion for questions (Are you...?) and 'not' for negatives (isn't, aren't). No auxiliary 'do' with 'be'.

The verb 'be' (am / is / are).label: Production
The verb 'be' (am / is / are).text: Speed introductions: name, origin, job, mood using be.

The verb 'have got' / 'have'.label: Possession
The verb 'have got' / 'have'.text: Teach 'have got' (BrE, spoken) and 'have' for possession: 'I've got a car / I have a car.' Present both forms.

The verb 'have got' / 'have'.label: Questions & negatives
The verb 'have got' / 'have'.text: 'have got' uses have as auxiliary (Have you got...? Haven't got); plain 'have' uses do (Do you have...?). Contrast briefly.

The verb 'have got' / 'have'.label: Production
The verb 'have got' / 'have'.text: Talk about possessions and family using have/have got.

Present simple (habits & facts).label: Third-person -s
Present simple (habits & facts).text: Drill the he/she/it -s ending, the main A1 difficulty. Use daily-routine verbs (works, lives, gets up).

Present simple (habits & facts).label: do/does for Q & neg
Present simple (habits & facts).text: Introduce auxiliary do/does for questions and don't/doesn't for negatives — and the bare infinitive after them.

Present simple (habits & facts).label: Production
Present simple (habits & facts).text: Survey classmates' daily habits, then report a partner's routine in the third person.

Present continuous (now).label: be + -ing
Present continuous (now).text: Form: am/is/are + verb-ing, for actions happening now. Mime activities and describe them live.

Present continuous (now).label: Contrast with present simple
Present continuous (now).text: Now (continuous) vs routine (simple): 'I usually walk, but today I'm taking the bus.' Sorting drill.

Present continuous (now).label: Production
Present continuous (now).text: Describe a busy 'people in a park' picture using is/are + -ing.

Imperative (commands & instructions).label: Bare infinitive
Imperative (commands & instructions).text: Use the base verb for instructions and classroom language: 'Open your books. Listen. Don't write.'

Imperative (commands & instructions).label: Negative & softening
Imperative (commands & instructions).text: Negative = 'Don't + verb'. Add 'please' to soften. Drill with a 'Simon says' game.

Imperative (commands & instructions).label: Production
Imperative (commands & instructions).text: Give a partner directions or a simple recipe in imperatives.

'there is' / 'there are'.label: Existence
'there is' / 'there are'.text: Teach 'there is' + singular, 'there are' + plural to say what exists in a place.
'there is' / 'there are'.ex: 'There is a market. There are two banks.'

'there is' / 'there are'.label: Negatives & questions
'there is' / 'there are'.text: There isn't / there aren't; Is there...? Are there...? Use with 'any' in questions/negatives.

'there is' / 'there are'.label: Production
'there is' / 'there are'.text: Describe a room or town: list what there is/are.

Adjective + noun order (a red car).label: Adjective before noun
Adjective + noun order (a red car).text: Unlike many languages, the adjective comes BEFORE the noun: 'a red car', not 'a car red'. Card-ordering drill.

Adjective + noun order (a red car).label: After 'be' too
Adjective + noun order (a red car).text: Adjectives also follow 'be': 'The car is red.' Both positions, same form.

Adjective + noun order (a red car).label: Production
Adjective + noun order (a red car).text: Describe objects placing the adjective correctly in both positions.

Adjectives are invariable (no plural -s).label: No agreement
Adjectives are invariable (no plural -s).text: English adjectives do not change for gender or number: 'a tall boy / two tall boys'. Contrast with the learner's L1.

Adjectives are invariable (no plural -s).label: Drill the contrast
Adjectives are invariable (no plural -s).text: Quick transformation: make the noun plural, keep the adjective the same.

Adjectives are invariable (no plural -s).label: Production
Adjectives are invariable (no plural -s).text: Describe groups of objects, resisting any urge to add -s to the adjective.

Possessive adjectives (my, your, his...).label: The set
Possessive adjectives (my, your, his...).text: Drill my, your, his, her, its, our, their + noun. They show who owns the thing.

Possessive adjectives (my, your, his...).label: his vs her
Possessive adjectives (my, your, his...).text: The form matches the OWNER's gender, not the object: 'Tom loves his sister', 'Anna loves her brother'. Targeted drill.

Possessive adjectives (my, your, his...).label: Production
Possessive adjectives (my, your, his...).text: Talk about family members' possessions using the right possessive.

Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.label: Near vs far, sing vs plural
Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.text: this/these = near; that/those = far. Singular vs plural. Use real objects and gestures.
Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.ex: 'this pen / these pens / that car / those cars'

Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.label: As adjective or pronoun
Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.text: Show both 'this book' (+noun) and 'This is mine' (alone). Quick contrast.

Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.label: Production
Demonstratives (this / that / these / th.text: Shopping role-play pointing at near and far items.

Subject pronouns (I, you, he...).label: Obligatory subject
Subject pronouns (I, you, he...).text: Drill I, you, he, she, it, we, they. English is not pro-drop: every clause needs a subject.

Subject pronouns (I, you, he...).label: 'I' and 'it'
Subject pronouns (I, you, he...).text: Capital 'I' always; 'it' for things, weather and time. Highlight he/she only for people.

Subject pronouns (I, you, he...).label: Production
Subject pronouns (I, you, he...).text: Replace names with pronouns when retelling who does what.

Object pronouns (me, you, him...).label: The object set
Object pronouns (me, you, him...).text: Drill me, you, him, her, it, us, them after verbs and prepositions.
Object pronouns (me, you, him...).ex: 'Call me. I see them. Give it to her.'

Object pronouns (me, you, him...).label: Subject vs object
Object pronouns (me, you, him...).text: Match pairs (I/me, he/him, they/them). Position: object pronouns come after the verb.

Object pronouns (me, you, him...).label: Production
Object pronouns (me, you, him...).text: Short dialogues replacing object nouns with pronouns.

Possessive pronouns (mine, yours...).label: Stand-alone possession
Possessive pronouns (mine, yours...).text: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs replace a possessive + noun: 'It's my book → It's mine.'

Possessive pronouns (mine, yours...).label: No noun after
Possessive pronouns (mine, yours...).text: Contrast adjective vs pronoun: 'my car' (+noun) vs 'mine' (alone). Transformation drill.

Possessive pronouns (mine, yours...).label: Production
Possessive pronouns (mine, yours...).text: Sort mixed-up belongings: 'This is mine, that's yours.'

Negation with 'not' / don't / doesn't.label: Two systems
Negation with 'not' / don't / doesn't.text: 'be' and modals add 'not' directly (isn't, can't); other verbs need don't/doesn't + base verb. Sort verbs into the two groups.

Negation with 'not' / don't / doesn't.label: Third person
Negation with 'not' / don't / doesn't.text: Drill doesn't (he/she/it) vs don't (I/you/we/they), with the bare infinitive after.

Negation with 'not' / don't / doesn't.label: Production
Negation with 'not' / don't / doesn't.text: Make true/false statements about yourself, then correct the false ones with negatives.

Adverbs of frequency (always, often, nev.label: A frequency scale
Adverbs of frequency (always, often, nev.text: Order always → usually → often → sometimes → rarely → never on a line. Link to routines.

Adverbs of frequency (always, often, nev.label: Position
Adverbs of frequency (always, often, nev.text: Mid-position: before the main verb but after 'be'. 'She often works late' / 'She is often late.'

Adverbs of frequency (always, often, nev.label: Production
Adverbs of frequency (always, often, nev.text: Class survey on habits; report frequencies.

Word order (SVO).label: Subject-Verb-Object
Word order (SVO).text: Establish the fixed S-V-O order with colour-coded cards. English relies on order, not case endings.

Word order (SVO).label: Manipulate
Word order (SVO).text: Rebuild scrambled sentences; show how changing order changes meaning ('The dog bites the man' is not the reverse).

Word order (SVO).label: Production
Word order (SVO).text: Write simple S-V-O sentences from pictures.

Yes/no questions (do / does, be).label: Two question types
Yes/no questions (do / does, be).text: With 'be'/modals, invert (Are you...? Can you...?); with other verbs, add Do/Does at the front.
Yes/no questions (do / does, be).ex: 'Do you like tea? / Are you tired?'

Yes/no questions (do / does, be).label: Short answers
Yes/no questions (do / does, be).text: Drill 'Yes, I do / No, I don't', 'Yes, she is / No, she isn't'. Match the auxiliary.

Wh- questions (what, where, when, who).label: Question word + auxiliary
Wh- questions (what, where, when, who).text: Wh- word first, then the yes/no question structure: 'Where do you live? What is this?'

Wh- questions (what, where, when, who).label: who as subject
Wh- questions (what, where, when, who).text: Note 'Who lives here?' needs no 'do' (who = subject). Brief contrast with object questions.

Wh- questions (what, where, when, who).label: Production
Wh- questions (what, where, when, who).text: Interview a partner with a set of wh- questions.

Basic connectors (and, but, or, because).label: Join ideas
Basic connectors (and, but, or, because).text: and (addition), but (contrast), or (choice), because (reason). Combine short sentences.

Basic connectors (and, but, or, because).label: because = reason
Basic connectors (and, but, or, because).text: Answer 'why?' with 'because + clause'. Drill cause-reason pairs.

Basic connectors (and, but, or, because).label: Production
Basic connectors (and, but, or, because).text: Write three linked sentences about your day using all four connectors.

Cardinal numbers (0–100).label: Build in steps
Cardinal numbers (0–100).text: 0–12 (irregular), 13–19 (-teen), 20–90 (-ty), then combine (twenty-one). Listening practice for -teen vs -ty.

Cardinal numbers (0–100).label: Hyphen & 'and'
Cardinal numbers (0–100).text: Write compound numbers with a hyphen (forty-five). Note BrE 'a hundred and five'.

Cardinal numbers (0–100).label: Production
Cardinal numbers (0–100).text: Exchange phone numbers, prices and ages aloud.

some / any.label: Affirmative vs Q/neg
some / any.text: 'some' in positive sentences, 'any' in questions and negatives. Use with plurals and uncountables.
some / any.ex: 'I have some bread. / Is there any milk?'

some / any.label: Offers & requests
some / any.text: Note 'some' in offers/requests ('Would you like some tea?'). Quick exception.

some / any.label: Production
some / any.text: Talk about what's in the fridge using some/any.

Possessive 's (Saxon genitive).label: 's for people
Possessive 's (Saxon genitive).text: Use 's to show possession, mainly with people and animals: 'Tom's car', 'the dog's tail'.

Possessive 's (Saxon genitive).label: Singular vs plural
Possessive 's (Saxon genitive).text: Singular noun + 's; plural noun ending in -s + apostrophe only (the students' books). Contrast drill.

Possessive 's (Saxon genitive).label: Production
Possessive 's (Saxon genitive).text: Describe who owns what in a family tree.

Zero article (general plurals & uncounta.label: No article for generalisations
Zero article (general plurals & uncounta.text: Drop 'the' when talking about things in general: 'I like dogs / Coffee is expensive.'

Zero article (general plurals & uncounta.label: Specific vs general
Zero article (general plurals & uncounta.text: Contrast 'Dogs are friendly' (general, no article) with 'The dogs next door bark' (specific). Sorting task.

Zero article (general plurals & uncounta.label: Production
Zero article (general plurals & uncounta.text: State general likes/dislikes with zero article.

Past simple (regular -ed).label: Q & neg with did
Past simple (regular -ed).text: Questions/negatives use did/didn't + base verb (no -ed): 'Did you work? / I didn't work.'

Past simple (regular -ed).label: Production
Past simple (regular -ed).text: Narrate last weekend with regular past verbs.

Past simple (irregular verbs).label: High-frequency list
Past simple (irregular verbs).text: Drill the most common irregulars (go/went, have/had, see/saw, make/made, take/took). Group by pattern where possible.

Past simple (irregular verbs).label: Same Q/neg rule
Past simple (irregular verbs).text: Questions and negatives still use did/didn't + base verb, so the irregular form appears only in affirmatives.

Past simple (irregular verbs).label: Production
Past simple (irregular verbs).text: Tell a short story of a past trip mixing regular and irregular verbs.

Past continuous.label: was/were + -ing
Past continuous.text: Action in progress in the past: 'At 8 p.m. I was watching TV.' Timeline work.

Past continuous.label: Interrupted action
Past continuous.text: Combine with past simple: 'I was cooking when the phone rang.' Past continuous = background, past simple = interruption.

Past continuous.label: Production
Past continuous.text: Describe what people were doing during an event (e.g. a power cut).

'going to' future (plans & predictions).label: be going to + verb
'going to' future (plans & predictions).text: Intentions and plans already decided: 'I'm going to study tonight.' Drill the form.

'going to' future (plans & predictions).label: Evidence predictions
'going to' future (plans & predictions).text: Also for predictions based on what we see now: 'Look at the clouds — it's going to rain.'

'going to' future (plans & predictions).label: Production
'going to' future (plans & predictions).text: Talk about weekend plans using 'going to'.

'will' future (decisions & predictions).label: Instant decisions
'will' future (decisions & predictions).text: Use 'will' for decisions made at the moment of speaking and offers: 'I'll help you. / I'll have the soup.'

'will' future (decisions & predictions).label: Predictions/opinions
'will' future (decisions & predictions).text: For opinions about the future after think/probably: 'I think it will rain.' Contrast with 'going to'.

'will' future (decisions & predictions).label: Production
'will' future (decisions & predictions).text: React to situations with spontaneous 'I'll...' offers.

Present perfect (experience & recent pas.label: have/has + past participle
Present perfect (experience & recent pas.text: Link past to now: life experience and recent results. 'I have visited Paris. / She has just arrived.'

Present perfect (experience & recent pas.label: ever / never / just / yet
Present perfect (experience & recent pas.text: Introduce the typical markers. Contrast with past simple + finished time ('yesterday' → past simple).

Present perfect (experience & recent pas.label: Production
Present perfect (experience & recent pas.text: 'Find someone who has ever...' class mingle.

Modals: can / can't (ability & permissio.label: can + base verb
Modals: can / can't (ability & permissio.text: Ability and permission: 'I can swim. Can I open the window?' No -s, no 'to'.

Modals: can / can't (ability & permissio.label: Negatives & questions
Modals: can / can't (ability & permissio.text: can't / cannot; questions by inversion (Can you...?). Pronunciation of can (weak) vs can't.

Modals: can / can't (ability & permissio.label: Production
Modals: can / can't (ability & permissio.text: Talk about skills and ask permission in role-plays.

Modals: must / have to (obligation).label: Two ways to say 'obligation'
Modals: must / have to (obligation).text: 'must' (speaker's authority/strong) and 'have to' (external rule). 'I must finish this. / I have to wear a uniform.'

Modals: must / have to (obligation).label: Negatives differ
Modals: must / have to (obligation).text: 'mustn't' = prohibition; 'don't have to' = no obligation. Crucial contrast drill.
Modals: must / have to (obligation).ex: 'You mustn't smoke' is not 'You don't have to smoke'

Modals: must / have to (obligation).label: Production
Modals: must / have to (obligation).text: List rules at school/work using must / have to.

Modals: should (advice).label: should + base verb
Modals: should (advice).text: Give advice and recommendations: 'You should rest. You shouldn't worry.'

Modals: should (advice).label: Soft vs strong
Modals: should (advice).text: Position 'should' as softer than 'must'. Drill advice for common problems.

Modals: should (advice).label: Production
Modals: should (advice).text: Agony-aunt activity: give advice with should/shouldn't.

Zero conditional (general truths & instr.label: Noticing in context
Zero conditional (general truths & instr.text: Hand out three short authentic texts that contain nothing but zero conditionals: a fire-drill notice, the instructions on a coffee machine, and four science facts. Learners underline every verb and answer one question only — what tense is used in each half of the sentence? Elicit the discovery that both clauses are present simple and that [will] appears nowhere.
Zero conditional (general truths & instr.ex: Support: one-page handout — fire-drill notice, coffee-machine instructions, four science facts.

Zero conditional (general truths & instr.label: Guided discovery: the if/when test
Zero conditional (general truths & instr.text: Put two pairs on the board — [If you press this button, the door opens.] / [When you press this button, the door opens.] against [If it rains, I will stay in.] / [When it rains, I will stay in.]. Ask learners which pair means the same thing twice. Draw the conclusion for them: when the result is automatic, [if] and [when] are interchangeable, and that swap is the test that separates this pattern from the first conditional they already know.

Zero conditional (general truths & instr.label: Controlled practice and punctuation
Zero conditional (general truths & instr.text: Run a substitution drill from a fixed frame — [If you ___ , it ___ .] — feeding in heat ice, drop a glass, forget to water plants. Then make each learner rewrite two sentences with the clauses reversed and correct only the punctuation: comma when the if-clause comes first, no comma when it comes second.
Zero conditional (general truths & instr.ex: Support: a set of twelve prompt cards, six facts and six machine actions.

Zero conditional (general truths & instr.label: Freer production: rules and instructions
Zero conditional (general truths & instr.text: In pairs, learners write six rules for a place they know — the school lab, a swimming pool, a shared kitchen — using an imperative result clause: [If the alarm rings, leave the building.] Require one sentence with [unless]. Correct two things only: any stray [will] and any missing third-person -s.

Comparatives (-er / more ... than).label: Short vs long adjectives
Comparatives (-er / more ... than).text: One syllable + -er (taller); two-plus syllables → more (more expensive). 'than' for the comparison.

Comparatives (-er / more ... than).label: Irregulars & spelling
Comparatives (-er / more ... than).text: good→better, bad→worse, far→further; double the consonant (big→bigger), -y→-ier (happy→happier).

Comparatives (-er / more ... than).label: Production
Comparatives (-er / more ... than).text: Compare two cities, phones or people.

Superlatives (the -est / the most).label: the + -est / most
Superlatives (the -est / the most).text: Short adjectives + -est (the tallest); long ones the most (the most expensive). Always with 'the'.

Superlatives (the -est / the most).label: Irregulars
Superlatives (the -est / the most).text: good→the best, bad→the worst, far→the furthest. Drill alongside comparatives.

Superlatives (the -est / the most).label: Production
Superlatives (the -est / the most).text: Rank a top-three list (films, places) using superlatives.

Adjective order (opinion-size-age-colour.label: A rough order
Adjective order (opinion-size-age-colour.text: When stacking adjectives: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → noun. 'a lovely big old house.'

Adjective order (opinion-size-age-colour.label: Two is plenty
Adjective order (opinion-size-age-colour.text: In real use, two or three adjectives is typical. Order familiar pairs (big red, nice old).

Adjective order (opinion-size-age-colour.label: Production
Adjective order (opinion-size-age-colour.text: Describe objects with two stacked adjectives in the natural order.

Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...).label: Same subject & object
Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...).text: Use myself, yourself, himself... when subject and object are the same: 'I cut myself.'

Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...).label: Emphasis use
Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...).text: Also for emphasis: 'I did it myself.' And 'by myself' = alone. Brief contrast.

Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...).label: Production
Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself...).text: Talk about things you do for yourself / by yourself.

'one' / 'ones' (substitution).label: Avoid repeating the noun
'one' / 'ones' (substitution).text: Use 'one/ones' to replace a countable noun already mentioned: 'I'll take the red one.'

'one' / 'ones' (substitution).label: With this/that & adjectives
'one' / 'ones' (substitution).text: 'this one, the big ones, a new one'. Drill substitution in shopping contexts.

'one' / 'ones' (substitution).label: Production
'one' / 'ones' (substitution).text: Shopping role-play choosing between items using one/ones.

Adverbs of manner (-ly).label: adjective + -ly
Adverbs of manner (-ly).text: Form manner adverbs from adjectives: quick→quickly, careful→carefully. They say HOW.

Adverbs of manner (-ly).label: Irregulars
Adverbs of manner (-ly).text: good→well, fast→fast, hard→hard. Note 'hardly' is not 'hard'. Sorting drill.

Adverbs of manner (-ly).label: Production
Adverbs of manner (-ly).text: Describe how people do actions (mime + adverb).

too / enough.label: Position differs
too / enough.text: 'too' before adjective (too small); 'enough' after adjective but before noun (big enough / enough money).
too / enough.ex: 'It's too expensive. / Is it big enough?'

too / enough.label: too much/many
too / enough.text: 'too much' + uncountable, 'too many' + plural. Contrast 'too' (excess) with 'enough' (sufficiency).

too / enough.label: Production
too / enough.text: Complain/comment about a room or meal using too/enough.

already / yet / just (with present perfe.label: Three markers
already / yet / just (with present perfe.text: 'just' = a moment ago; 'already' = sooner than expected (positive); 'yet' = up to now (questions/negatives, end position).
already / yet / just (with present perfe.ex: 'I've just eaten. Have you finished yet?'

already / yet / just (with present perfe.label: Position
already / yet / just (with present perfe.text: just/already mid-position; yet at the end. Drill placement.

already / yet / just (with present perfe.label: Production
already / yet / just (with present perfe.text: Report task progress using all three.

Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.label: Noticing in context
Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.text: Hand out a short diary page describing one week — appointments, a birthday, a holiday, a train — with every time phrase in bold. Learners underline only the preposition in each phrase and sort the phrases into three piles headed AT, ON, IN, with a fourth pile for phrases that have no preposition at all. Give no rule before the sorting is finished.
Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.ex: Support: one-page diary text “Kate’s week” with the fifteen time phrases in bold.

Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.label: Guided discovery: precision ladder
Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.text: Elicit from the sorted piles that the three prepositions form a ladder of precision: AT for a point (at 7 o’clock, at midnight, at the weekend in British English), ON for a whole day or date (on Monday, on 5 June, on Christmas Day), IN for anything longer (in June, in 2026, in the summer). Then test the ladder on the two traps: at night against in the morning, and on Friday morning, where the named day outranks the part of the day.
Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.ex: Support: three-column wall chart AT / ON / IN, with a separate box for FOR / SINCE.

Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.label: Controlled practice: for vs since
Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.text: Drill the pair against the present perfect the class already knows. Say a date or a length of time and require a full sentence in reply: “2020” gives “I have lived here since 2020”, “three years” gives “I have lived here for three years”. Correct on the spot every “since three years” and make the learner say back which of the two is a length and which is a starting point.

Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.label: Freer production: my timeline
Prepositions of time (in, on, at, for, s.text: Each learner draws a timeline of their own life and writes eight sentences about it, using at least one AT, one ON, one IN, one FOR, one SINCE and one AGO, plus one sentence with last or next and no preposition. Pairs exchange timelines and correct only the prepositions before the sentences are read aloud.

Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.label: Noticing in context
Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.text: Project a labelled picture of a flat and read out eight short statements about it: the keys are in the drawer, the poster is on the wall, somebody is waiting at the door. Learners point at the object each time and write only the preposition they hear, so that attention goes to the small word rather than to the vocabulary.
Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.ex: Material: one A3 picture of a flat with numbered objects, plus a listening script of eight statements.

Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.label: Guided discovery: in / on / at
Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.text: Build a three-column poster on the board — in for an enclosed space or an area, on for a surface or a line, at for a point or an institution seen as a function — and have learners sort twenty cards into the columns: the box, the wall, the bus stop, London, the second floor, work, bed, the door. Then present the contrast pairs in the car versus on the bus, at school versus in the school, and in / on / at the corner, and make learners say what changes in the meaning, not which one is correct.
Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.ex: Material: twenty word cards plus the three-column poster, kept on the wall for the whole unit.

Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.label: Controlled practice: movement
Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.text: Drill the movement set with mime: one learner acts out an instruction — walk into the room, get off the chair, go out of the door, walk across the classroom, go past the desk, climb onto the table — while the class calls out the preposition. Correct only the preposition, and insist on the two-word forms out of and in front of, which learners tend to shorten.

Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.label: Freer production: directions
Prepositions of place & movement (in, on.text: In pairs, learners describe the route from the school to their home in six sentences and then describe their own bedroom in six more, using at least ten different prepositions. Collect the errors on the board and correct them as a class, paying particular attention to any added preposition before home, abroad and downstairs.

Question words + auxiliary.label: Consolidate wh- + aux
Question words + auxiliary.text: Drill how, why, how much/many, how long with the right auxiliary and tense. 'How long did you stay?'

Question words + auxiliary.label: Subject vs object Qs
Question words + auxiliary.text: Contrast 'Who saw you?' (subject, no do) with 'Who did you see?' (object, with do).

Question words + auxiliary.label: Production
Question words + auxiliary.text: Build an interview mixing subject and object questions.

Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.label: Order a narrative
Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.text: Use first, then, next, after that, finally to sequence events. Arrange a scrambled story.
Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.ex: 'First I woke up, then I had breakfast...'

Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.label: before/after + -ing
Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.text: Introduce 'before/after + -ing' for same-subject sequencing ('After eating, I left').

Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.label: Production
Sequencers (first, then, after that, fin.text: Describe a daily routine or recipe with sequencers.

Defining relative clauses (who, which, t.label: who/which/that
Defining relative clauses (who, which, t.text: who for people, which for things, that for both. They identify which one. 'The man who lives here.'

Defining relative clauses (who, which, t.label: Subject vs object relative
Defining relative clauses (who, which, t.text: Show object relatives where the pronoun can be omitted: 'the book (that) I bought'. Brief drill.

Defining relative clauses (who, which, t.label: Production
Defining relative clauses (who, which, t.text: Define people/objects in a guessing game using relative clauses.

Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).label: Noticing in context
Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).text: Read aloud a short conversation between two neighbours in which every second turn ends in a tag: “You're the new tenant, aren't you?”, “The lift isn't working, is it?”. Learners underline the two-word ending of each sentence and say, for each one, whether the speaker is checking something or genuinely asking.
Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).ex: Support: an eight-line dialogue with the six tags printed in bold.

Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).label: Guided discovery
Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).text: Put four statements on the board, two positive and two negative, and elicit the tags. Mark each half with a plus or a minus so the class formulates the rule itself: a positive statement takes a negative tag, a negative statement takes a positive tag. Then add a second column for the auxiliary — copy the one already there, or bring in do, does or did when the statement has none.
Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).ex: Support: a two-column grid, statement / tag, with eight rows to complete.

Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).label: Controlled practice
Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).text: Rapid oral drill: you read the statement, the class answers with the tag alone. Slot in the special cases every third item — I'm late…, Let's start…, Open the window…, There is a problem…, Nobody phoned… Correct two errors on the spot: [am I not] in place of [aren't I], and any negative tag after never, hardly, nobody or nothing.

Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).label: Freer production with intonation
Question tags (isn't it? don't you?).text: In pairs, learners guess three facts about their partner and check each one with a tag, using a falling voice when they are fairly sure and a rising voice when they are really asking. Correct polarity and auxiliary first; then ask each pair to report which of their tags were genuine questions and which were only seeking agreement.

Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).label: Countable vs uncountable
Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).text: 'many' + plural, 'much' + uncountable; 'a lot of' for both. 'much/many' favour questions/negatives.
Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).ex: 'How much time? How many people? a lot of money'

Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).label: Positive → a lot of
Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).text: Prefer 'a lot of' in positive statements ('I have a lot of work'); 'much/many' in questions/negatives.

Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).label: Production
Quantifiers (much / many / a lot of).text: Talk about quantities (work, friends, money) choosing correctly.

Ordinal numbers (first, second...).label: Form & spelling
Ordinal numbers (first, second...).text: first, second, third (irregular), then -th (fourth, fifth...). Used for dates, floors, rankings.

Ordinal numbers (first, second...).label: Dates
Ordinal numbers (first, second...).text: BrE 'the fifth of June' / AmE 'June fifth'. Drill saying dates.

Ordinal numbers (first, second...).label: Production
Ordinal numbers (first, second...).text: Give birthdays and rank a top list with ordinals.

Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).label: A decision routine
Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).text: Build a flowchart: countable? specific/known? general plural or uncountable? → choose a/the/zero. Apply to a text.
Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).ex: 'I bought a car. The car is red. Cars are useful.'

Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).label: Fixed phrases
Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).text: Note article-free expressions (go to bed, at school, by car) and 'the' with unique/known nouns.

Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).label: Production
Articles: a/the/zero (systematic review).text: Correct a text where all articles have been removed.

Compound nouns (bus stop, toothbrush).label: Noun + noun
Compound nouns (bus stop, toothbrush).text: The first noun describes the second: 'a bus stop' = a stop for buses. Build and decode compounds.

Compound nouns (bus stop, toothbrush).label: First noun stays singular
Compound nouns (bus stop, toothbrush).text: The modifying noun is usually singular: 'a five-star hotel', 'a ten-minute walk'. Drill the pattern.

Compound nouns (bus stop, toothbrush).label: Production
Compound nouns (bus stop, toothbrush).text: Label objects and places using compound nouns.

Present perfect continuous.label: have been + -ing
Present perfect continuous.text: Emphasise duration of a recent/ongoing activity: 'I've been studying for three hours.'

Present perfect continuous.label: Activity vs result
Present perfect continuous.text: Contrast with present perfect simple: continuous stresses the activity/duration; simple stresses the completed result.

Present perfect continuous.label: Production
Present perfect continuous.text: Explain why you look tired/busy using the continuous.

Past perfect.label: had + past participle
Past perfect.text: An action before another past action: 'When I arrived, they had already left.' Timeline work.

Past perfect.label: Sequencing the past
Past perfect.text: Combine with past simple to show order. Drill 'because ... had ...' explanations.

Past perfect.label: Production
Past perfect.text: Narrate a past event explaining what had happened before.

Future continuous.label: will be + -ing
Future continuous.text: An action in progress at a future time: 'This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Rome.'
Future continuous.ex: 'Don't call at 8 — we'll be having dinner.'

Future continuous.label: Polite enquiry
Future continuous.text: Also for polite questions about plans: 'Will you be using the car tonight?'

Future continuous.label: Production
Future continuous.text: Describe what you'll be doing at set times next week.

used to / would (past habits).label: Past habits & states
used to / would (past habits).text: 'used to + base verb' for repeated past actions and past states no longer true: 'I used to live in Lagos.'

used to / would (past habits).label: would for repeated actions
used to / would (past habits).text: 'would' can replace 'used to' for repeated past ACTIONS (not states): 'Every summer we would visit...'.

used to / would (past habits).label: Production
used to / would (past habits).text: Describe childhood habits with used to / would.

Passive voice (present & past).label: be + past participle
Passive voice (present & past).text: Focus on the action/result, not the doer: 'English is spoken here. The window was broken.'

Passive voice (present & past).label: by + agent
Passive voice (present & past).text: Add 'by' only when the doer matters. Transform active → passive across present and past.

Passive voice (present & past).label: Production
Passive voice (present & past).text: Describe a process (how something is made) in the passive.

First conditional (real future).label: if + present, will + base
First conditional (real future).text: Real/likely future condition: 'If it rains, we'll stay home.' Note the present tense after 'if'.

First conditional (real future).label: unless / when
First conditional (real future).text: Introduce 'unless' (= if not) and contrast 'if' (uncertain) with 'when' (certain). Drill paired clauses.

Second conditional (hypothetical).label: if + past, would + base
Second conditional (hypothetical).text: Unreal/imaginary present or future: 'If I had money, I would travel.' The past form signals unreality.

Second conditional (hypothetical).label: were for all persons
Second conditional (hypothetical).text: In the if-clause, 'were' is used for all persons in careful English ('If I were rich'). Contrast with first conditional.

Second conditional (hypothetical).label: Production
Second conditional (hypothetical).text: Discuss imaginary situations ('What would you do if...?').

Reported speech (statements).label: Backshift
Reported speech (statements).text: Move tenses one step back after a past reporting verb: present→past, will→would, 'I'm tired' → 'He said he was tired.'
Reported speech (statements).ex: 'I live here' becomes 'She said she lived there.'

Reported speech (statements).label: Shift pronouns & time words
Reported speech (statements).text: Adjust pronouns and references (now→then, tomorrow→the next day, here→there). Transformation drill.

Reported speech (statements).label: Production
Reported speech (statements).text: Report what classmates said in an earlier survey.

Gerunds vs infinitives (verb patterns).label: Verb-dependent
Gerunds vs infinitives (verb patterns).text: Some verbs take -ing (enjoy, finish, avoid), others take to-infinitive (want, decide, hope). Sort common verbs.

Gerunds vs infinitives (verb patterns).label: Meaning change verbs
Gerunds vs infinitives (verb patterns).text: Note pairs that change meaning (stop doing vs stop to do; remember doing vs remember to do).

Gerunds vs infinitives (verb patterns).label: Production
Gerunds vs infinitives (verb patterns).text: Talk about likes/plans using the correct pattern after each verb.

Past ability (could / was able to / mana.label: Noticing in context
Past ability (could / was able to / mana.text: Read out a short rescue story containing four ability forms: “She could swim before she could walk”, “The fire spread quickly, but everyone was able to escape”, “I couldn't open the emergency door” and “We could hear people shouting”. Ask learners to underline every way of talking about ability and to write beside each one whether it describes a skill over a period or one particular moment.
Past ability (could / was able to / mana.ex: Support: a ten-line printed narrative with the four ability forms in bold, plus a two-column grid headed “over a period / one moment”.

Past ability (could / was able to / mana.label: Guided discovery of the one-occasion rule
Past ability (could / was able to / mana.text: Put the two sentences “She could swim at four” and “He could escape from the burning house” side by side and ask the class which one sounds wrong and why. Lead them to state the rule themselves: could is fine for a general skill, but a single successful action needs was/were able to or managed to. Write the rule on the board in the learners' own words.

Past ability (could / was able to / mana.label: Controlled practice with the two exceptions
Past ability (could / was able to / mana.text: Drill twelve short prompts orally, mixing general skills, single successes, negatives and perception verbs. Insist that the negative loses the restriction, so “I couldn't open the door” is correct, and that see, hear, smell, feel, understand and remember keep could even at one precise moment.
Past ability (could / was able to / mana.ex: Support: a set of twelve prompt cards, each marked with a small icon for skill, one-off success, negative or perception.

Past ability (could / was able to / mana.label: Freer production: the difficult journey
Past ability (could / was able to / mana.text: In pairs, learners tell the story of a journey or a day when almost everything went wrong, using at least three ability forms and one managed to. Correct only two things at feedback stage: any could used for a single successful action, and the pattern after manage and succeed, which must be manage to do and succeed in doing.

Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).label: Noticing in context
Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).text: Read a short dialogue containing eight phrasal verbs: get up, turn off, look after, look forward to, break down, find out, put off, run into. Learners underline every verb + particle unit and answer one question only — could you guess the meaning from the two words alone? Do not give translations yet.
Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).ex: Support: a twelve-line dialogue, target items in bold, plus a strip of the eight verbs cut up for sorting.

Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).label: Guided discovery: four types
Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).text: Learners sort the underlined verbs into four columns using two tests: does the verb take an object, and can a noun object stand after the particle? Elicit the four labels — intransitive, transitive separable, transitive inseparable, three-part — and have each pair add one more verb of their own to every column.
Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).ex: Support: a four-column grid with turn off and look after already placed as models.

Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).label: Controlled practice: pronoun drill
Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).text: Drill the three-step transformation aloud: turn off the light → turn the light off → turn it off. Then contrast the inseparable pattern: look after the baby → look after her, with no middle step. Stop the class the moment anyone produces [turn off it] or [look her after] and rebuild the correct order on the board.

Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).label: Freer production: register switch
Phrasal verbs (separable & inseparable).text: In pairs, learners write a five-line informal message using six phrasal verbs, then rewrite it as a formal e-mail replacing each one with its Latinate equivalent — put off / postpone, find out / discover, give up / abandon, throw away / discard. Correct word order first, register second.

Reported questions, commands & requests.label: Noticing the word-order shift
Reported questions, commands & requests.text: Put four pairs on the board, the direct question above and the reported version below: “Where do you live?” / He asked me where I lived. Ask learners to draw an arrow showing that the auxiliary do disappears and that the subject moves back in front of the verb, then to cross out the question mark themselves. Do not re-teach backshift here: treat it as known and keep the whole focus on order and punctuation.
Reported questions, commands & requests.ex: Support: handout of eight direct/reported pairs, one pair per line, wh- questions only, the auxiliary printed in grey so it can be struck through.

Reported questions, commands & requests.label: Guided discovery of if / whether
Reported questions, commands & requests.text: Give six yes/no questions with no question word and ask pairs to report them; they will feel that a link word is missing. Supply if and whether, then add two items containing “or not” and one after a preposition, such as “It depends on ___ he comes”, so that the class discovers for itself that only whether works in those two positions.

Reported questions, commands & requests.label: Controlled practice: verb + object + to
Reported questions, commands & requests.text: Call out orders and polite requests at speed — “Sit down!”, “Don't be late!”, “Could you open the window?” — and have the class answer chorally: He told me to sit down, He told me not to be late, She asked me to open the window. Correct two things only: the personal object after tell and ask, and the position of not immediately before to.
Reported questions, commands & requests.ex: Support: card set of twenty spoken prompts, ten orders and ten polite requests, plus a second set for advise, warn, remind, invite and beg.

Reported questions, commands & requests.label: Freer production: relaying a message
Reported questions, commands & requests.text: In threes, learner A reads a dialogue card containing two questions, one order and one request, and reports it orally to B, who writes the four reported sentences down; C checks the punctuation. Collect the written versions and correct only four things: word order in the questions, if/whether, the missing personal object after tell, and any stray question mark.

Gradable vs non-gradable adjectives.label: Two kinds
Gradable vs non-gradable adjectives.text: Gradable (big, hot, tired) take 'very/quite'; non-gradable/extreme (huge, freezing, exhausted) take 'absolutely/totally'.

Gradable vs non-gradable adjectives.label: Matching intensifiers
Gradable vs non-gradable adjectives.text: Drill which intensifier fits which type. 'absolutely delicious', not 'very delicious' (in careful use).

Gradable vs non-gradable adjectives.label: Production
Gradable vs non-gradable adjectives.text: React to experiences choosing gradable/non-gradable adjectives + intensifier.

-ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring).label: Feeling vs cause
-ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring).text: -ed describes how you feel (bored, interested); -ing describes the thing causing it (boring, interesting).

-ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring).label: Common pairs
-ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring).text: Drill excited/exciting, tired/tiring, surprised/surprising in matched sentences.

-ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring).label: Production
-ed vs -ing adjectives (bored / boring).text: Describe experiences and your reactions using both forms.

Relative pronouns (whose, where, when).label: Beyond who/which
Relative pronouns (whose, where, when).text: 'whose' = possession ('the man whose car...'), 'where' = place, 'when' = time. Extend defining clauses.

Relative pronouns (whose, where, when).label: Choose the right pronoun
Relative pronouns (whose, where, when).text: Match pronoun to function (owner/place/time). Combine sentence pairs.

Relative pronouns (whose, where, when).label: Production
Relative pronouns (whose, where, when).text: Describe people and places using whose/where/when.

Reciprocal pronouns (each other).label: Mutual action
Reciprocal pronouns (each other).text: 'each other / one another' for a two-way action: 'They love each other.' Contrast with reflexive (themselves).

Reciprocal pronouns (each other).label: With prepositions
Reciprocal pronouns (each other).text: 'talk to each other, look at one another'. Brief drill on placement.

Adverbs of degree (quite, really, a bit).label: Strengthen or soften
Adverbs of degree (quite, really, a bit).text: Scale modifiers: a bit / quite / really / extremely before adjectives. 'It's quite cold / really cold.'

Adverbs of degree (quite, really, a bit).label: Register & nuance
Adverbs of degree (quite, really, a bit).text: Note BrE 'quite' can mean 'fairly' (quite good) or 'completely' (quite right) by adjective type. Brief awareness.

Adverbs of degree (quite, really, a bit).label: Production
Adverbs of degree (quite, really, a bit).text: Give graded opinions on films/food using degree adverbs.

Comparative & superlative adverbs.label: more / most + adverb
Comparative & superlative adverbs.text: Most adverbs use more/most: 'more carefully, the most quickly'. Short ones add -er/-est (faster, hardest).

Comparative & superlative adverbs.label: Irregulars
Comparative & superlative adverbs.text: well→better→best, badly→worse→worst, far→further. Drill alongside adjective comparison.

Comparative & superlative adverbs.label: Production
Comparative & superlative adverbs.text: Compare how people do things ('She works harder than...').

Linking adverbs (however, therefore).label: Logical links in writing
Linking adverbs (however, therefore).text: however (contrast), therefore/so (result), in addition (adding), for example. Position at clause start with a comma.

Linking adverbs (however, therefore).label: Punctuation
Linking adverbs (however, therefore).text: Show semicolon/full stop before, comma after. Contrast with conjunctions (but/so) that join within one sentence.

Linking adverbs (however, therefore).label: Production
Linking adverbs (however, therefore).text: Improve a choppy paragraph by adding linking adverbs.

Non-defining relative clauses.label: Extra information
Non-defining relative clauses.text: Add non-essential detail between commas: 'My brother, who lives in Paris, is a doctor.' The clause can be removed.
Non-defining relative clauses.ex: 'The book, which I loved, is out of print.'

Non-defining relative clauses.label: No 'that', no omission
Non-defining relative clauses.text: Use who/which (not that) and never omit the pronoun. Contrast with defining clauses.

Non-defining relative clauses.label: Production
Non-defining relative clauses.text: Add extra information about known people/things in commas.

Time clauses (when, while, as soon as).label: Present for future
Time clauses (when, while, as soon as).text: After when, as soon as, until, before, after — use the present (not 'will') for future time: 'I'll call when I arrive.'

Time clauses (when, while, as soon as).label: while + continuous
Time clauses (when, while, as soon as).text: 'while' often pairs with continuous for background ('while I was cooking'). Drill clause combinations.

Time clauses (when, while, as soon as).label: Production
Time clauses (when, while, as soon as).text: Plan a sequence of future actions with time clauses.

Reason & result (because, so, since).label: Cause vs consequence
Reason & result (because, so, since).text: because/since/as introduce a reason; so introduces a result. 'I stayed in because it rained / It rained, so I stayed in.'

Reason & result (because, so, since).label: Register & position
Reason & result (because, so, since).text: 'since/as' often start the sentence for known reasons; 'because' usually follows. Brief contrast.

Reason & result (because, so, since).label: Production
Reason & result (because, so, since).text: Explain decisions giving reason and result.

Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.label: Same subject → to
Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.text: Same subject uses 'to / in order to + base verb': 'I came here to learn English.'
Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.ex: 'She left early to catch the train.'

Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.label: Different subject → so that
Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.text: Different subjects need 'so that + clause': 'I spoke slowly so that everyone could understand.'

Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.label: Production
Purpose clauses (to / in order to / so t.text: State goals, switching between 'to' and 'so that'.

few / a few / little / a little.label: Countable vs uncountable
few / a few / little / a little.text: a few/few + plural; a little/little + uncountable. 'a few friends', 'a little time'.

few / a few / little / a little.label: With vs without 'a'
few / a few / little / a little.text: 'a few/a little' = some (positive nuance); 'few/little' = almost none (negative nuance). Contrast pairs.

few / a few / little / a little.label: Production
few / a few / little / a little.text: Describe resources you have using the four forms with the right nuance.

both / either / neither.label: Two-item quantifiers
both / either / neither.text: both = the two together; either = one or the other; neither = not one and not the other.

both / either / neither.label: Agreement & structure
both / either / neither.text: 'both + plural verb'; 'neither/either + singular verb'. 'both...and', 'either...or', 'neither...nor'. Drill pairs.

Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).label: Singular or plural verb?
Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).text: Collective nouns (team, government, family) take a singular OR plural verb in BrE depending on whether the group acts as one body or as individuals.
Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).ex: 'The team is strong' vs 'The team are arguing'

Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).label: BrE vs AmE
Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).text: Note AmE prefers the singular ('The team is...'). Drill choosing the verb form by meaning and variety.

Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).label: Production
Abstract & collective nouns (agreement).text: Write sentences about organisations, choosing agreement to match the intended sense.

Article nuances (institutions, generalis.label: Institution vs building
Article nuances (institutions, generalis.text: Zero article for the institutional purpose (go to hospital/school/prison) vs 'the' for the physical place (go to the hospital to visit).
Article nuances (institutions, generalis.ex: 'in hospital' (as a patient) vs 'at the hospital' (the building)

Article nuances (institutions, generalis.label: Generic 'the'
Article nuances (institutions, generalis.text: Contrast generic plural (zero) with generic 'the' + singular for species/inventions ('The tiger is endangered'). Brief drill.

Article nuances (institutions, generalis.label: Production
Article nuances (institutions, generalis.text: Edit a text fixing institution vs building and generic uses.

Future perfect.label: will have + past participle
Future perfect.text: An action completed before a point in the future: 'By next year, I'll have graduated.'

Future perfect.label: With 'by' / 'by the time'
Future perfect.text: Pair with 'by' + time or 'by the time + present'. Contrast with future simple/continuous on a timeline.

Future perfect.label: Production
Future perfect.text: Set goals: what you'll have achieved by certain future dates.

Third conditional (past unreal).label: if + past perfect, would have + pp
Third conditional (past unreal).text: Imagining a different past: 'If I had studied, I would have passed.' Both clauses look back and are unreal.
Third conditional (past unreal).ex: 'If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed it.'

Third conditional (past unreal).label: Contracted forms
Third conditional (past unreal).text: Drill the heavily contracted spoken forms ('If I'd known, I'd have called'). Listening practice.

Third conditional (past unreal).label: Production
Third conditional (past unreal).text: Express regrets about past decisions in the third conditional.

Mixed conditionals.label: Cross time references
Mixed conditionals.text: Mix a past condition with a present result, or vice versa: 'If I had saved money (past), I would be rich now (present).'
Mixed conditionals.ex: 'If I were taller, I would have made the team.'

Mixed conditionals.label: Identify the time of each clause
Mixed conditionals.text: Analyse which clause is past and which present, then match the right forms. Sorting drill.

Mixed conditionals.label: Production
Mixed conditionals.text: Link a past cause to a present consequence about your own life.

Passive (all tenses; passive reporting).label: Extend across tenses
Passive (all tenses; passive reporting).text: Build the passive in perfect, continuous and modal forms: 'has been done, is being built, must be finished.'

Passive (all tenses; passive reporting).label: Reporting passive
Passive (all tenses; passive reporting).text: Impersonal reporting: 'It is said that... / He is believed to be...'. Useful for objective/academic register.

Passive (all tenses; passive reporting).label: Production
Passive (all tenses; passive reporting).text: Rewrite a news item using passive and reporting structures.

Modals of deduction (must/might/can't ha.label: Certainty scale (present)
Modals of deduction (must/might/can't ha.text: must (sure it's true), might/could/may (possible), can't (sure it's false): 'He must be tired. / It can't be true.'

Modals of deduction (must/might/can't ha.label: Past deduction
Modals of deduction (must/might/can't ha.text: modal + have + past participle: 'must have left, might have forgotten, can't have seen.' Drill present vs past.

Modals of deduction (must/might/can't ha.label: Production
Modals of deduction (must/might/can't ha.text: Speculate about a mystery picture/situation, present and past.

Causative (have/get something done).label: have + object + past participle
Causative (have/get something done).text: Someone else does the job for you: 'I had my car repaired. / I'm getting my hair cut.'

Causative (have/get something done).label: have vs get; misfortune
Causative (have/get something done).text: 'get' is more informal; also for unwanted events ('She had her bag stolen'). Drill the word order.

Causative (have/get something done).label: Production
Causative (have/get something done).text: Describe services you arrange using the causative.

'wish' / 'if only'.label: Three patterns
'wish' / 'if only'.text: wish + past (present regret: 'I wish I had a car'); wish + past perfect (past regret: 'I wish I had studied'); wish + would (annoyance: 'I wish you would listen').

'wish' / 'if only'.label: Map wish to conditionals
'wish' / 'if only'.text: Link the backshift logic to second/third conditionals. Sorting by time and meaning.

'wish' / 'if only'.label: Production
'wish' / 'if only'.text: Express present and past regrets and complaints with wish/if only.

Adjectives as nouns (the rich, the unemp.label: the + adjective = group
Adjectives as nouns (the rich, the unemp.text: 'the + adjective' names a whole group of people, plural in sense: 'the rich, the elderly, the homeless.'

Adjectives as nouns (the rich, the unemp.label: Plural agreement
Adjectives as nouns (the rich, the unemp.text: These take a plural verb and no -s: 'The unemployed are...'. Contrast with 'a rich person'.

Adjectives as nouns (the rich, the unemp.label: Production
Adjectives as nouns (the rich, the unemp.text: Write social-issue sentences using adjective-as-noun groups.

Order & modification of adjectives (inte.label: Fine-tune intensity
Order & modification of adjectives (inte.text: Layer intensifiers/downtoners: 'a remarkably well-designed, surprisingly cheap phone.' Match intensifier to adjective type.

Order & modification of adjectives (inte.label: Hyphenated pre-modifiers
Order & modification of adjectives (inte.text: Compound modifiers before nouns are hyphenated ('a well-known author', 'a five-year-old child'). Drill.

Order & modification of adjectives (inte.label: Production
Order & modification of adjectives (inte.text: Write a product review with precisely modified adjectives.

Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything,.label: some-/any-/no-/every- families
Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything,.text: Build the grid (someone/anyone/no one/everyone; something/anything...). some- in positives, any- in Q/neg.

Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything,.label: Singular agreement & they
Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything,.text: They take a singular verb ('Everyone is here') but singular 'they' for reference ('Someone left their bag').

Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything,.label: Production
Indefinite pronouns (someone, anything,.text: Describe a scene/situation using indefinite pronouns.

'it' & 'there' as dummy subjects.label: Two empty subjects
'it' & 'there' as dummy subjects.text: 'there' introduces existence ('There is a problem'); 'it' fills the subject slot for weather, time, distance and to delay a clause ('It is hard to say').

'it' & 'there' as dummy subjects.label: Anticipatory 'it'
'it' & 'there' as dummy subjects.text: 'It' postpones a long subject: 'It is surprising that he left' (= That he left is surprising). Transformation drill.

'it' & 'there' as dummy subjects.label: Production
'it' & 'there' as dummy subjects.text: Comment on situations using anticipatory 'it' and existential 'there'.

Adverb position & focus adverbs (only, e.label: Position changes meaning
Adverb position & focus adverbs (only, e.text: Focus adverbs (only, even, just) attach to what follows: 'Only I saw her' vs 'I only saw her' vs 'I saw only her.' Compare meanings.

Adverb position & focus adverbs (only, e.label: Place next to the focus
Adverb position & focus adverbs (only, e.text: Put the adverb immediately before the word it limits. Drill by shifting 'only' through a sentence.

Adverb position & focus adverbs (only, e.label: Production
Adverb position & focus adverbs (only, e.text: Write sentences where moving 'only' changes the meaning, and gloss each.

Negative & limiting adverbs (hardly, rar.label: Near-negative meaning
Negative & limiting adverbs (hardly, rar.text: hardly/scarcely/barely (= almost not), rarely/seldom (= almost never). The clause is positive in form.

Negative & limiting adverbs (hardly, rar.label: No double negative
Negative & limiting adverbs (hardly, rar.text: Because they are already negative in sense, don't add 'not': 'I hardly ever go' (not 'don't hardly').

Negative & limiting adverbs (hardly, rar.label: Production
Negative & limiting adverbs (hardly, rar.text: Describe infrequent habits using rarely/seldom/hardly ever.

Concession (although, despite, in spite.label: Clause vs noun
Concession (although, despite, in spite.text: although/though/even though + clause; despite/in spite of + noun or -ing. 'Although it rained...' / 'Despite the rain...'.
Concession (although, despite, in spite.ex: 'In spite of being tired, she continued.'

Concession (although, despite, in spite.label: Transform between them
Concession (although, despite, in spite.text: Rewrite 'although + clause' as 'despite + noun/-ing' and back. Drill the structural switch.

Concession (although, despite, in spite.label: Production
Concession (although, despite, in spite.text: Concede a point in an argument using all three forms.

Cause & result connectors (consequently,.label: Formal links
Cause & result connectors (consequently,.text: due to/owing to + noun (cause); consequently/as a result/therefore (result, linking adverbs). Build a formal register set.

Cause & result connectors (consequently,.label: due to vs because of
Cause & result connectors (consequently,.text: 'due to' traditionally follows 'be' ('The delay was due to fog'); 'because of' modifies a verb. Brief usage note.

Cause & result connectors (consequently,.label: Production
Cause & result connectors (consequently,.text: Write a cause-effect paragraph in formal register.

Cleft sentences (It was... / What...).label: Two cleft types
Cleft sentences (It was... / What...).text: It-cleft highlights one element ('It was John who called'); wh-cleft fronts a clause ('What I need is time'). Mark the focus.

Cleft sentences (It was... / What...).label: Build from a neutral sentence
Cleft sentences (It was... / What...).text: Take 'John broke the window' and produce both clefts emphasising different parts. Transformation drill.

Cleft sentences (It was... / What...).label: Production
Cleft sentences (It was... / What...).text: Re-emphasise facts in a short text using clefts.

Participle clauses.label: Reduce a clause
Participle clauses.text: Shorten a clause to a participle: 'Feeling tired, she left' (= Because she felt tired). Present (-ing) for active, past (-ed) for passive.

Participle clauses.label: Same-subject rule
Participle clauses.text: The participle's implied subject must match the main clause. Combine sentence pairs.

Participle clauses.label: Production
Participle clauses.text: Condense a descriptive paragraph using participle clauses.

Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).label: With or without 'of'
Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).text: General: 'most people' (no of); specific: 'most of the people' (+ of + the/possessive/pronoun). Contrast the two.
Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).ex: 'All children / all of the children in this class'

Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).label: Agreement with 'none of'
Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).text: 'none of' + plural can take singular (formal) or plural (informal) verb. Drill the structures.

Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).label: Production
Quantifiers review (all/most/none of).text: Report survey results using all/most/some/none of.

Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.label: Pack the noun phrase
Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.text: Combine pre-modifiers (adjectives, nouns) and post-modifiers (prepositional phrases, relative and participle clauses) around one head noun.
Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.ex: 'the recently published report on climate change'

Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.label: Compress for headlines/academia
Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.text: Condense a full sentence into a dense noun phrase. Practise on news and academic style.

Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.label: Production
Complex noun phrases (pre/post-modificat.text: Turn three short sentences into a single rich noun phrase.

Nominalisation (academic style).label: Verb/adjective → noun
Nominalisation (academic style).text: Turn processes into nouns for an abstract, objective register: 'decide → the decision to', 'fail → the failure of'.

Nominalisation (academic style).label: Information density
Nominalisation (academic style).text: Rewrite verbal sentences as nominal ones, noting the more formal, compact effect. Drill on academic extracts.

Nominalisation (academic style).label: Production
Nominalisation (academic style).text: Reformulate an informal paragraph into nominalised academic prose.

Inversion after negative adverbials (Nev.label: Fronting triggers inversion
Inversion after negative adverbials (Nev.text: Front a negative/limiting adverbial and invert subject and auxiliary: 'Never have I seen such a thing. / Not only did he lie, but...'.

Inversion after negative adverbials (Nev.label: Common triggers
Inversion after negative adverbials (Nev.text: Drill the set: never, rarely, seldom, hardly...when, no sooner...than, not only, little, only then. Transform from neutral sentences.

Inversion after negative adverbials (Nev.label: Production
Inversion after negative adverbials (Nev.text: Rewrite emphatic statements with fronted negatives + inversion.

Subjunctive & 'were to' / 'be to'.label: Mandative subjunctive
Subjunctive & 'were to' / 'be to'.text: Base verb after demand/suggest/insist + that: 'I suggest that he be informed. / It is essential that she arrive on time.'

Subjunctive & 'were to' / 'be to'.label: Hypothetical 'were to' / planning 'be to'
Subjunctive & 'were to' / 'be to'.text: 'If I were to tell you...' (tentative future); 'be to' for official plans/instructions ('You are to report at 9'). Contrast uses.

Subjunctive & 'were to' / 'be to'.label: Production
Subjunctive & 'were to' / 'be to'.text: Write formal recommendations and tentative hypotheses using these forms.

Future in the past.label: Past viewpoint, later action
Future in the past.text: From a past moment, refer to something then still future: 'was going to, would, was about to, was to.' 'He was going to call but forgot.'

Future in the past.label: Choose the right form
Future in the past.text: Match nuance: intention (was going to), destiny (was to), imminence (was about to). Sorting drill.

Future in the past.label: Production
Future in the past.text: Narrate past plans and how they turned out.

Modal nuances (habits, willingness, crit.label: Beyond core meanings
Modal nuances (habits, willingness, crit.text: 'will/would' for typical behaviour ('He will sit there for hours'); 'would' for past willingness/refusal ('The car wouldn't start'); 'might/could have' for criticism ('You could have told me').

Modal nuances (habits, willingness, crit.label: Read the context
Modal nuances (habits, willingness, crit.text: Identify the nuance (habit, willingness, reproach, annoyance) from context. Analysis of authentic lines.

Modal nuances (habits, willingness, crit.label: Production
Modal nuances (habits, willingness, crit.text: Express criticism and characteristic behaviour using these modal nuances.

Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.label: Subtle tense choices
Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.text: Fine-tune present perfect vs past simple, and simple vs continuous, for connotation: finished vs relevant-now, permanent vs temporary, complete vs in progress.
Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.ex: 'I lived there' vs 'I have lived there' vs 'I have been living there'

Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.label: Connotation drills
Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.text: Compare near-minimal pairs and articulate the difference in meaning/emphasis. Discussion-based analysis.

Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.label: Production
Advanced aspect (perfect vs simple contr.text: Write a short reflective text exploiting aspectual contrasts deliberately.

Adjective complementation (keen on, eage.label: Adjective + preposition / clause
Adjective complementation (keen on, eage.text: Many adjectives take a fixed preposition or pattern: 'keen on -ing, eager to do, aware that, capable of -ing.' Group by pattern.

Adjective complementation (keen on, eage.label: Preposition vs infinitive
Adjective complementation (keen on, eage.text: Contrast adjectives taking 'of + -ing' vs 'to + infinitive'. Drill collocations.

Adjective complementation (keen on, eage.label: Production
Adjective complementation (keen on, eage.text: Describe attitudes and abilities using correctly complemented adjectives.

Cohesion & substitution (do so, such).label: Avoid repetition
Cohesion & substitution (do so, such).text: Use substitution to refer back: 'do so / do it / do that' for verb phrases; 'such' and 'so' for ideas. 'I asked him to leave and he did so.'

Cohesion & substitution (do so, such).label: Register of 'do so'
Cohesion & substitution (do so, such).text: 'do so' is formal; 'do it/that' more neutral. Drill substitution in connected text.

Cohesion & substitution (do so, such).label: Production
Cohesion & substitution (do so, such).text: Edit a repetitive paragraph using substitution devices.

Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).label: Leave out the recoverable
Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).text: Omit repeated words after auxiliaries or 'to': 'I haven't finished but she has (finished). / I'd love to (come).'
Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).ex: 'You can go if you want to.'

Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).label: Coordination ellipsis
Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).text: Drop repeated subjects/verbs in coordination ('She bought the tickets and (she) booked the hotel'). Drill restoration.

Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).label: Production
Ellipsis (auxiliary & to-infinitive).text: Tighten a wordy text by ellipting recoverable elements.

Epistemic adverbs (apparently, presumabl.label: Mark your certainty
Epistemic adverbs (apparently, presumabl.text: Signal how sure you are: certainly, presumably, apparently, supposedly, allegedly (decreasing certainty/distance). Place on a scale.

Epistemic adverbs (apparently, presumabl.label: Source distancing
Epistemic adverbs (apparently, presumabl.text: 'allegedly/supposedly/reportedly' distance you from a claim you don't fully endorse. Drill in reporting contexts.

Epistemic adverbs (apparently, presumabl.label: Production
Epistemic adverbs (apparently, presumabl.text: Report unverified news, calibrating commitment with the right adverb.

Comment & viewpoint adverbs (frankly, te.label: Comment on the whole clause
Comment & viewpoint adverbs (frankly, te.text: Sentence adverbs frame the statement: 'Frankly, I disagree. / Technically, it's illegal. / Unfortunately, we lost.'

Comment & viewpoint adverbs (frankly, te.label: Position & punctuation
Comment & viewpoint adverbs (frankly, te.text: Usually sentence-initial with a comma. Distinguish comment adverbs (frankly = I speak frankly) from manner adverbs (he spoke frankly).

Comment & viewpoint adverbs (frankly, te.label: Production
Comment & viewpoint adverbs (frankly, te.text: Add stance to statements using comment and viewpoint adverbs.

Fronting & emphasis.label: Move an element to the front
Fronting & emphasis.text: Front objects, complements or adverbials for emphasis/cohesion: 'That I can't accept. / Down the road came a car.'
Fronting & emphasis.ex: 'Such was his anger that he left.'

Fronting & emphasis.label: With and without inversion
Fronting & emphasis.text: Some fronting triggers inversion ('Down came the rain'), some doesn't ('This book I love'). Sort examples.

Fronting & emphasis.label: Production
Fronting & emphasis.text: Rewrite neutral sentences with marked fronting for effect.

Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).label: Range of clefts
Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).text: Beyond basic clefts: 'All I want is..., The reason (why)..., The place where..., What happened was...'. Mark the focus precisely.
Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).ex: 'The thing that bothers me is the cost.'

Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).label: Choose the structure for focus
Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).text: Match cleft type to the element emphasised and the discourse flow. Transformation drills.

Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).label: Production
Cleft & pseudo-cleft (advanced).text: Restructure an argument's key points with varied clefts.

Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.label: Formal cohesion set
Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.text: Organise written argument with moreover, furthermore, nevertheless, conversely, hence, thereby, whereas. Group by function (add/contrast/result).
Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.ex: 'The plan is costly; nevertheless, it is necessary.'

Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.label: Register & precision
Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.text: Distinguish near-synonyms (however vs nevertheless vs nonetheless) and avoid spoken markers in formal writing. Drill selection.

Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.label: Production
Discourse markers (moreover, nevertheles.text: Structure a formal argumentative paragraph with precise markers.

Hedging & academic register.label: Soften claims
Hedging & academic register.text: Use hedges for cautious, academic tone: 'may/might, tend to, it appears that, to some extent, arguably.' 'This may suggest that...'.
Hedging & academic register.ex: 'The data appear to indicate a trend.'

Hedging & academic register.label: Balance hedge & stance
Hedging & academic register.text: Combine hedging with cautious commitment; avoid both overclaiming and excessive vagueness. Edit overstated sentences.

Hedging & academic register.label: Production
Hedging & academic register.text: Rewrite bold assertions as appropriately hedged academic claims.

Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.label: Choose 's or of
Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.text: 's for living/personified possessors and time ('a day's work'); 'of' for inanimate/abstract and long phrases. Compare nuance.
Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.ex: 'the company's policy' vs 'the policy of the company'

Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.label: Double genitive
Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.text: 'a friend of mine', 'a painting of Picasso's' (one of his works) vs 'a painting of Picasso' (depicting him). Disambiguation drill.

Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.label: Production
Genitive & possession nuances (of vs 's;.text: Edit phrases choosing the genitive that fits sense and rhythm.

Marked noun forms (foreign plurals: crit.label: Latin/Greek plurals
Marked noun forms (foreign plurals: crit.text: criterion/criteria, phenomenon/phenomena, datum/data, analysis/analyses, index/indices. Treat as pairs to master.

Marked noun forms (foreign plurals: crit.label: Shifting usage
Marked noun forms (foreign plurals: crit.text: Note items drifting to regular usage ('data' as singular mass noun in many fields). Discuss register and field norms.

Marked noun forms (foreign plurals: crit.label: Production
Marked noun forms (foreign plurals: crit.text: Use these nouns with correct agreement in academic sentences.

All tenses & aspects (controlled product.label: The whole system
